query: For HfNbTaTiZr refractory high-entropy alloy, earlier studies separately examined tensile creep at 1250 °C, microhardness changes during cold rolling, elastic moduli from 293 to 1100 K, and hardening after aging at 600–800 °C. However, these findings do not provide a unified explanation of the alloy’s stress–strain and thermoelastic behavior. Thermal expansion is also relevant because mismatch can produce thermal stresses during composite solidification and potentially affect strength. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain the unresolved behavior? Specify a controlled comparison that would isolate the governing cause, observations predicted relative to a baseline, the relevant temperature and response boundaries, how the earlier findings support the hypothesis, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Thermoelastic and mechanical property variations in the HfNbTaTiZr refractory high-entropy alloy are primarily driven by thermal expansion mismatch stresses that develop as a result of microstructural changes during thermal aging.
generation.intervention: Thermal aging treatment at intermediate temperatures (600–800 °C) versus the as‐cast condition.
generation.conditions: In situ tests conducted over a broad temperature range—from room temperature (∼293 K) up to high temperatures (∼1250 °C), with controlled environmental conditions to isolate thermal expansion effects.
generation.structural_mediator: Microstructure architecture changes (e.g., slight lattice distortion, potential nano-precipitate or phase segregation formation) that modify the alloy’s effective thermal expansion coefficient.
generation.mechanism: Thermal aging induces microstructural rearrangements that change the local thermal expansion behavior, leading to internal stresses (thermal expansion mismatch). These stresses interact with dislocations and the elastic lattice, thereby modulating both the stress–strain response and the thermoelastic properties over operational temperature ranges.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as‐cast baseline, thermally aged samples will exhibit altered thermal expansion behavior with measurable internal stresses, reflected in changes to elastic moduli and a shift in the stress–strain curves. For example, increased internal stresses and modified creep response are expected at 600–800 °C and at temperatures up to 1250 °C.
generation.baseline: As‐cast HfNbTaTiZr alloy with uniform thermal expansion and standard stress–strain responses at the same temperatures.
generation.boundary: Observations are confined to the temperature regime from room temperature (∼293 K) up to 1250 °C and are compared between as‐cast and thermally aged (600–800 °C) states.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative effect of the thermal expansion mismatch stresses on the overall mechanical behavior remains uncertain, as interactions with dislocation dynamics and other strengthening mechanisms could complicate the direct attribution.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set in the as‐cast condition and another set subjected to thermal aging at 600–800 °C. Conduct in situ diffraction (e.g., neutron or synchrotron X-ray diffraction) and dilatometry during controlled uniaxial tensile tests over the temperature range from room temperature up to 1250 °C to monitor lattice strain evolution and elastic modulus changes.
measurements: Elastic moduli (from in situ diffraction combined with mechanical testing)
Lattice strain and microstructural evolution (from diffraction peak shifts and broadening)
Creep strain rates at high temperatures
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the thermal aging does not result in a measurable difference in thermal expansion behavior or internal stress (i.e., if the as‐cast and aged samples exhibit statistically indistinguishable elastic moduli, lattice strain evolution, and creep responses), then the hypothesis that thermal expansion mismatch is the governing cause of the altered stress–strain and thermoelastic behavior is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: It has been confirmed that σi of equiatomic CoCrNi is 218 MPa. The strengthening contributions from solid-solution hardening, HDI hardening, and precipitation hardening are calculated to be ∼49 MPa, ∼800 MPa, and ∼1115 MPa, respectively, (as presented in Supplementary Note 2), the total yield strength estimated by Eq. (1) would be 2182 MPa, in reasonable agreement with the measured 2000 MPa. Another feature for the designed alloy is that a promising uniform elongation of ∼13% is still achieved even at the strongly strengthened state. It is believed that this behavior is also originated from pronounced work-hardening rates induced during the tension process. Specifically, the strain-hardening rate curve shows that the specimens perform high strain-hardening rates at high stress levels (Fig. 1a). To correlate the work-hardening behavior with the underlying deformation mechanisms upon uniaxial tensile loading, the microstructural evolution of aging alloy after deformation is observed by SXRD and TEM.

AbstractNowadays refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are regarded as great candidates for the replacement of superalloys at high temperature. To design a RHEA, one must understand the pros and cons of every refractory element. However, the elemental effect on mechanical properties remains unclear. In this study, the subtraction method was applied on equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloys to discover the role of each element, and, thus, HfMoNbTaTiZr, HfNbTaTiZr, HfMoTaTiZr, HfMoNbTiZr, HfMoNbTaZr, and HfMoNbTaTi were fabricated and analyzed. The microstructure and mechanical properties of each alloy at the as-cast state were examined. The solid solution phase formation rule and the solution strengthening effect are also discussed. Finally, the mechanism of how Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr affect the HfMoNbTaTiZr alloys was established after comparing the properties of these alloys.Keywords: high-entropy alloys, refractory high-entropy alloys, alloys design, elevated-temperature yield strength, solid solution strengthening effect

reading.lever: Combine in situ diffraction and dilatometry on as‐cast vs. thermally aged HfNbTaTiZr to quantify thermal expansion mismatch induced stresses.
reading.why: This integrated approach directly isolates the effect of thermal expansion mismatch on stress–strain and thermoelastic behavior, addressing the gap unifying previous separate findings.
